text: Dolly, a female Finn-Dorset sheep born on 5 July 1996 and died on 14 February 2003, was the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell. She was created at the Roslin Institute in Scotland by Keith Campbell, Ian Wilmut, and colleagues from the University of Edinburgh and PPL Therapeutics, using a technique called somatic cell nuclear transfer, where a nucleus from a mammary gland cell was transferred into an unfertilized egg cell that had its nucleus removed. The resulting hybrid cell was stimulated to divide and, when it developed into a blastocyst, was implanted into a surrogate mother. Dolly was the first clone produced from a cell taken from an adult mammal, proving that genes in a mature, differentiated somatic cell can revert to an embryonic totipotent state and develop into a whole organism. Although not the first animal ever cloned—John Gurdon had previously used adult somatic cells to clone African clawed frogs in 1958—Dolly gained widespread media attention as the first such clone from an adult mammal. She lived at the Roslin Institute throughout her life, where she was bred with a Welsh Mountain ram and produced six lambs: Bonnie in April 1998, twins Sally and Rosie in 1999, and triplets Lucy, Darcy, and Cotton in 2000. In 2001, at age four, she developed arthritis, which was treated with anti-inflammatory drugs, and by 2003, she had a progressive lung disease, specifically ovine pulmonary adenocarcinoma (Jaagsiekte), caused by the retrovirus JSRV. No link between her cloning and the disease was found, as similar cases occurred in other sheep in the flock. Dolly was euthanized at six years old, which is shorter than the typical 11–12-year lifespan of a Finn Dorset, though her telomeres were found to be short, leading some to speculate she had a genetic age of six. However, Roslin scientists found no evidence of advanced aging or health defects from cloning. After her death, her body was preserved via taxidermy and displayed at the National Museum of Scotland. In 2016, a study of 13 cloned sheep, including four from the same cell line as Dolly, found no long-term health issues beyond minor osteoarthritis, concluding there was no detrimental effect of cloning on aged offspring. Following Dolly’s success, many large mammals were cloned, including pigs, deer, horses, and bulls, though some attempts, like cloning argali, failed. Cloning efficiency was initially very low—Dolly was the only adult lamb from 277 attempts—and Wilmut later stated nuclear transfer may never be efficient for human use. By 2014, Chinese scientists achieved 70–80% success rates in cloning pigs, and by 2016, Sooam Biotech was producing 500 cloned embryos daily, while commercial pet cloning services like Viagen charged $50,000 for a dog, $30,000 for a cat, and $85,000 for a horse. Cloning has potential applications in preserving endangered species and reviving extinct ones; in 2009, scientists cloned the Pyrenean ibex, the first extinct animal to be cloned, though the newborn died shortly after birth due to lung defects. In 2016, four clones of Dolly—Daisy, Debbie, Dianna, and Denise—were alive and healthy at nine years old, and were later euthanized in 2017 after research showed they were aging normally. Scientific American noted that Dolly’s main legacy was in advancing stem cell research, including the discovery of induced pluripotent stem cells. In 2000, researchers cloned a lamb named Diana with a human gene for alpha 1-antitrypsin, which was activated in her mammary gland to produce therapeutic milk. In 2018, Chinese scientists created the first cloned primates, Zhong Zhong and Hua Hua, using the same method as Dolly. In 2019, five gene-edited cloned monkeys were created using CRISPR-Cas9, intended for medical research. In 2003, Belgian artist Dominique Goblet published a comic strip titled “2004 Apparition de Dolly dans la campagne anglaise” about her.
